claims.text: The onset of premelting in equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles is governed by thermodynamically driven Cu surface segregation.
Cu surface segregation forms a low-melting, Cu-rich shell.
The Cu-rich shell nucleates surface melting below the melting onset of a compositionally homogeneous particle of the same size.
The initial approximately 10 nm equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are chemically random at room temperature.
Elevated temperature causes Cu to migrate to the nanoparticle surface.
Cu has the lowest bulk melting point among the constituent elements.
Cu has the lowest surface energy among the constituent elements.
Surface-segregated Cu forms a liquid-like shell during heating.
The Cu-rich shell lowers the premelting temperature by reducing the surface-energy barrier to melting.
Particles with Cu-enriched surfaces will exhibit liquid-layer formation and morphological fluctuations at approximately 100 K below compositionally homogeneous particles of the same size.
Rapid quenching from synthesis can suppress Cu surface segregation in equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Annealing at 600 K can induce measurable Cu surface segregation.
The proposed comparison is restricted to equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles 5–20 nm in diameter under inert or vacuum conditions.
The expected melting-point depression has an uncertainty of approximately ±50 K.
The extent and kinetics of Cu segregation may vary with particle size and synthesis history.
